children.text: Badoc Church is the parish church of St. John the Baptist in the town of Badoc at the southern end of Ilocos Norte, a Marian shrine that enshrines the statue of La Virgen Milagrosa, said to have drifted in from the sea in a wooden box around 1620. It was raised to a minor basilica in 2018 and is also known as the church where the painter Juan Luna was baptized.

The official name of Badoc Church is the Minor Basilica and Parish of Saint John the Baptist. It is in Badoc, the southernmost town in Ilocos Norte, and because it enshrines La Virgen Milagrosa de Badoc (the Miraculous Virgin) as a diocesan shrine, it is also called by that name. According to Wikipedia it was built in the 17th century and became an independent parish in 1714 when it separated from the parish of St. Nicholas of Tolentino in neighboring Sinait. In 1980 a historical marker of the National Historical Institute (NHI) was installed, and there is a record that Pope Francis gave it minor basilica status in 2018. It is about 39 km from Laoag and about 445 km from Manila.

The reason this church draws pilgrims is the story of the Virgin statue. According to tradition, persecuted Catholics in Nagasaki set a statue of the Virgin and one of Christ adrift in wooden boxes during the Tokugawa shogunate, and it is said to be one of the statues that survived when the shogunate destroyed churches in 1614. The statues came ashore around 1620 on the beach of Paguetpet on the border of Sinait and Badoc, and Badoc fishermen are said to have taken the Virgin while Sinait fishermen took the statue of Christ. A legend about which side's fishermen could move each statue is told as well, and Sinait's Christ statue is enshrined as the Santo Cristo Milagroso of Sinait Church. The Badoc Virgin received a canonical coronation on May 31, 2018, and the church was raised to a minor basilica that same year.

The architecture is Spanish colonial Baroque. Like other Baroque churches in the province, it has thick buttresses lined along the side walls to withstand earthquakes and a single-nave plan. One travel article describes twelve buttresses on each side of a white facade built of brick and lime, and says the floor mixes green, ochre and cream machuca tiles with red Vigan tiles. The altar and pulpit are turquoise and gold, and the decorated retablo behind the altar is carved in detail and painted gold. There are modern reinforcements, but original brick sections remain in places. The bell tower is said to stand separately in the compound, away from the front entrance.

The open-air worship area behind the church is also worth seeing. Past low, wide arches there are two sunlit prayer spaces, and in one is a replica of the Virgin with an incense pot and a candle rack. One article cited this as an example of the syncretic character of Philippine Christianity. Records say the painter Juan Luna was baptized at this church in 1857, so a route that pairs it with the nearby Juan Luna museum is common. This guide is based on Wikipedia and travel articles, and I could not confirm Mass times or entry rules, so check with the parish before you visit.

blocks.title: The statue of La Virgen Milagrosa

children.text: A life-size statue enshrined at the center of the altar, venerated as the patroness of the Diocese of Laoag. As a Marian shrine, it draws a steady stream of the faithful at prayer. Keep quiet in front of the statue and do not disturb people who are praying.
The carved, gilded wall behind the altar draws the eye. The turquoise-and-gold altar and pulpit complement each other splendidly. Follow the signs as to whether photography is allowed.

blocks.title: Twelve buttresses and the white facade

children.text: The facade is white, and thick buttresses line the side walls to withstand earthquakes. One article reads the plant growing on the eave above the door as a symbol of life and rebirth. Around sunset the long shadows on the side walls make for good photos.

blocks.title: Floor of machuca and Vigan tiles

children.text: The floor of green, ochre and cream machuca tiles mixed with red Vigan tiles carries the feel of an old church. Some tiles are worn, so walk carefully.

blocks.title: The open-air worship area behind the church

children.text: Past a wide arch there are two sunlit prayer spaces and a replica of the Virgin. You can see how incense and candles blend with folk belief. Check the on-site guidance before taking photos.

blocks.title: The church where Juan Luna was baptized

children.text: Records say the painter Juan Luna was baptized in this church on October 27, 1857. The Juan and Antonio Luna Museum, related to his brother Antonio Luna, is in town and worth seeing with the church.

blocks.title: The shore where the Virgin landed and its chapel

children.text: On the Paguetpet shore, where the statue is said to have landed, there is a small chapel, and the beach has been named La Virgen Milagrosa Beach. There is a record that you can rent a floating bamboo cottage at the beach for about
for 4 hours.

blocks.title: The minor basilica status and the coronation

children.text: The canonical coronation on May 31, 2018, and the elevation to minor basilica in the same year were major turning points for this church. The date of the elevation differs by source, such as December 16 or November 30, so check the parish information.
Take a bus or van heading south to Badoc from Laoag. It is about 39 km from Laoag, and you should check the travel time locally.
Take a tricycle from Badoc town to the church. Look at the plaza in front of the church and the facade first.
Go inside and quietly see the altar and the Virgin, and admire the retablo.
Look around the open-air worship area behind the church and the replica Virgin.
Visit the nearby Juan and Antonio Luna Museum. Admission is known to be free, but check its opening days.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town.
Look around Paguetpet Beach, where the Virgin is said to have landed, or Badoc Island, then return to Laoag.
Tourist access may be restricted during Mass and events, so ask the parish.

items.title: Church pilgrimage route in southern Ilocos Norte
items.subtitle: Sinait and Badoc in one day

children.text: Go to Sinait and visit the church that holds the Santo Cristo Milagroso (the statue of Christ).
Go to Badoc and look around the church in front of the statue of La Virgen Milagrosa.
Have lunch in town and visit the Luna museum.
See the chapel by the shore and the sea, then return to Laoag.
This is a pilgrimage route that follows the story of two statues that came ashore separately from the same sea.
There are direct flights from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Laoag International Airport. Airlines and times vary by season, so check.
You can also take an overnight bus from Manila (Cubao and others) to Laoag and get off on the road near Badoc. Tell the driver to let you off in Badoc.
It is about 445 km from Manila to Badoc. The bus is known to take about
9–11 hours
It lies about 39 km south of Laoag. Take a bus running between Vigan and Laoag and get off on the road near Badoc town.
From the road to the church is a short tricycle ride.
One guide describes Badoc as about halfway between Vigan and Laoag, about
1 hour
away by bus.
The church and the Luna museum are close to each other, so you can walk or take a tricycle.
For the beach and Badoc Island, use a tricycle or motorcycle taxi. Agree on the fare including waiting time.

You can visit the church all year, but the November–May dry season is easier for getting around. As a Marian shrine it draws believers throughout the year, and it can get crowded especially around the Virgin's feast days and Holy Week.
In the June–October rainy season, typhoons and heavy rain make coastal travel difficult. Switch to a church-and-museum plan and put off the beach and Badoc Island until a day with good weather.

A visit in the morning is quietest and photographs best. In the afternoon, strong sunlight reflects off the white facade and flattens photos, so early morning or sunset is recommended. Sunday Mass hours are crowded with local worshippers, so it is easier to sightsee on a weekday.

Badoc is easy to cover as a day trip, so most visitors stay in Laoag or Vigan. If you want to enjoy the beach, you can look for beachside lodging near Badoc Island, but it is small, so check in advance.

You can easily find Ilocos foods such as bagnet and empanada at restaurants in town and along the road. At the beach, another option is to rent a floating cottage and eat there. Prices differ by restaurant, so check first.

Badoc is a small municipality of about 33,000 people (2024 census), divided into 31 barangays. The town's history is said to begin in 1572, when Spanish missionaries and soldiers made camp at the mouth of the Badoc River. Because the town is small, tourism infrastructure is modest, and the church and museum are within walking distance of each other, which suits a half-day plan. With one more day, you can also take in the coast and the surfing spot at Badoc Island.
A church is a place of worship. Enter in clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and keep quiet during Mass.
Mass and event times change, so check the parish notices and decide your visiting time.
There may be a line in front of the Virgin, so wait your turn and follow the guidance on photography.
Combining the church and the Luna museum fits comfortably in half a day.
Dates differ by source, such as Juan Luna's baptism record and the date of the minor basilica elevation, so give priority to the explanations on site.
At the beach, watch for waves and rip currents, and do not go far out without a life vest.
Bring a little cash, water and a hat.
A wide-angle lens helps for photos of the churchyard and facade; check the signs first before photographing the interior.
The interior of the church is where Mass and prayer take place. Avoid loud voices, flash photography and short clothing.
Tourist access may be restricted during Mass times and event periods.
I could not confirm the church's opening hours and entry rules, so ask the parish before you go.
Travel along the coast can be dangerous in typhoon season, so check the weather.
Sources differ on the minor basilica elevation and on the architect, so refer to the on-site notices.
There is little shade at midday and it is hot. Drink plenty of water.
